questions.q: What is the key difference between archiving and deletion, as this lesson defines them?
options: There is no real difference — they're two names for the same operation
Deletion permanently removes data no longer needed at all; archiving moves data out of the active working set while still preserving it for potential future retrieval
Archiving only applies to custom objects, while deletion only applies to standard objects
Archiving happens automatically on a schedule, while deletion always requires manual action
questions.explain: Archiving preserves data's retrievability while removing it from the active, frequently-queried working set; deletion removes data the organization has decided it no longer needs at all.

questions.q: In the four-step archiving sequence this lesson describes, what comes immediately before the data is actually removed from the active org?
options: Extraction only, with no other steps required
Notifying all org users by email
Backup, followed by a relationship-impact check
Disabling the object's page layout
questions.explain: The sequence is extract, back up as close to the point of deletion as possible, check relationship impact on parent/child records, and only then remove the data — backup and relationship analysis both have to happen before removal.

questions.q: Why is a backup described as the real safety net for an archiving project, rather than relying on the Recycle Bin?
options: Because the Recycle Bin automatically deletes all data immediately with no retention period at all
Because the Recycle Bin only applies to Big Objects
Because backups are legally required for every Salesforce org regardless of archiving plans
Because the Recycle Bin is a short-term undo mechanism, not an archive, and doesn't serve as a reliable long-term recovery point
questions.explain: The Recycle Bin is meant for short-term, routine undo, not as a dependable archive — which is why a real backup taken close to the point of deletion is the actual safety net for an archiving project.

questions.q: What problem does PK chunking solve that ordinary field-value-based chunking doesn't handle well?
options: At very large scale (hundreds of millions of records), filtering by field value stops being a practical primary chunking strategy, so PK chunking splits the extract by record Id instead
It encrypts extracted data automatically
It replaces Bulk API entirely with a faster proprietary tool
It automatically deletes records as they are extracted
questions.explain: PK chunking is specifically a technique for combating slow performance on very large-scale extracts, chunking by the record's primary key (Id) rather than a business field, once ordinary field-value-based chunking stops scaling well.

questions.q: Why does the relationship-impact-check step need to happen before any records are removed in an archiving project?
options: Because Salesforce requires a signed form before any deletion can occur

Because a record being archived might be a parent to records that aren't being archived, and removing it without checking could orphan related data, breaking reports, rollups, or integrations that assume the relationship still exists
Because relationship checks are only needed for custom objects, never standard ones
Because it determines which Salesforce edition the org needs
questions.explain: Deletion can break parent-to-child and child-to-parent relationships elsewhere in the org, so analyzing that impact before removal is necessary to avoid orphaning data that other processes depend on.
